items.prompt: Per L1's Scenario, why did the suite grow from 4 minutes to 38 minutes without anyone deciding to slow it down?
choices: Every new test added its own time to one long serial line, and nobody counteracted that growth as tests kept getting added
The team switched to a slower programming language partway through the year
CI hardware got progressively slower over the course of the year
Someone deliberately added artificial delays to every test
items.explanation: Running serially, total runtime is just the sum of every test's time. Each individually reasonable new test adds to that sum, so the suite slows down by simple addition unless something actively counteracts it, like parallelization.
items.reference:
🐢 4 min a year ago → 38 min today, same team, same CI budget
➕ No single bad decision — just serial addition, test by test

Why: a suite's runtime grows by simple arithmetic unless parallelization actively counteracts it.

Nobody noticed any change in behavior at all

items.prompt: Per L1, what does parallelization/sharding fix, and what does quarantine fix?
choices: Sharding fixes runtime by splitting the suite across workers; quarantine fixes chronic flakiness by moving confirmed-flaky tests out of the blocking suite

Neither one is described as fixing anything in L1 — both are only described in L2
items.explanation: L1 pairs each technique with a distinct target: sharding addresses the growing wall-clock time problem, and quarantine addresses the trust-eroding flakiness problem, which are related but different failure modes.
items.reference:
⚡ Sharding → fixes runtime
🧯 Quarantine → fixes trust/noise

Why: a suite can be slow without being noisy, or noisy without being slow — each technique targets a different symptom.

items.prompt: Per L1, why is quarantine not simply 'keep rerunning until it's green'?

items.explanation: L1 draws a sharp line between the habitual 'rerun and hope' reflex (which hid a real bug) and quarantine, which is a deliberate, tracked decision to stop a specific test from blocking merges.
items.reference:
⚡ Sharding → fixes runtime
🧯 Quarantine → fixes trust/noise

Why: a suite can be slow without being noisy, or noisy without being slow — each technique targets a different symptom.

items.reference:
🔀 Sharding — split across workers
🔒 Isolation — outcome doesn't depend on other tests
🧯 Quarantine — non-blocking, tracked track

items.prompt: Per L2, what does sharding a suite across 4 workers actually change about wall-clock time?
choices: It makes wall-clock time close to whatever the slowest worker takes, instead of the sum of every test

items.explanation: Sharding doesn't speed up any single test — it changes what determines total time from 'the sum of everything' to 'the slowest concurrent slice,' which is why it can keep runtime close to flat as test count grows.
items.reference:
1200 tests → 4 workers → ~300 tests each
wall-clock ≈ slowest worker, not the sum

Why: sharding changes what determines total time, not how fast any individual test runs.

items.prompt: Complete runIsolated(maxRequests, callCount), which simulates callCount concurrent calls against their OWN fresh limiter each (never shared), and returns how many were allowed. Use createLimiter(maxRequests) fresh per call, exactly like L3's runConcurrentlyAgainstIsolatedLimiters. Every call should be allowed, since each gets its own counter starting at 0.

tests.description: 4 isolated calls against maxRequests=1 are all allowed
tests.expr: (async () => { const result = await runIsolated(1, 4); return expect(result).toBe(4); })()

tests.description: 10 isolated calls against maxRequests=0 are still all allowed, since limit only blocks a SHARED counter
tests.expr: (async () => { const result = await runIsolated(0, 3); return expect(result).toBe(0); })()

items.explanation: Each call constructs its own createLimiter(maxRequests), so every call is the first call against a counter starting at 0 -- with maxRequests=1, every one of the 4 calls is independently allowed; with maxRequests=0, every one is independently blocked, since even the first call against a 0-limit fails. This is L3's isolated-fixture fix: nothing shared means nothing to interleave on, regardless of concurrency.
items.reference:
🔒 Each call gets its own createLimiter -- nothing shared
✅ Outcome is deterministic per call, independent of run order

Why: isolation removes the possibility of interleaving entirely, rather than trying to make interleaving safe.

items.prompt: Same runIsolated(maxRequests, callCount) as before. Confirm the count of allowed calls only ever depends on maxRequests (0 blocks everything since each isolated limiter starts fresh at its own limit), never on callCount for maxRequests=1.

tests.description: 1 isolated call against maxRequests=1 is allowed
tests.expr: (async () => { const result = await runIsolated(1, 1); return expect(result).toBe(1); })()

tests.description: 20 isolated calls against maxRequests=1 are ALL allowed, since none share a counter
tests.expr: (async () => { const result = await runIsolated(1, 20); return expect(result).toBe(20); })()

items.explanation: Because every call constructs its own limiter, callCount has no effect on the allowed count when maxRequests=1 -- all 20 calls are independently the first call against their own fresh counter, so all 20 are allowed. This is the direct contrast with the shared-limiter version, where increasing concurrent calls against ONE counter would start blocking calls past the limit.
items.reference:
🔒 Each call gets its own createLimiter -- nothing shared
✅ Outcome is deterministic per call, independent of run order

Why: isolation removes the possibility of interleaving entirely, rather than trying to make interleaving safe.

items.prompt: Complete routeTests(testIds, quarantined), a simplified version of L3's routing check. `quarantined` is a Set of test ids. Return { blocking, nonBlocking } where blocking contains every id NOT in quarantined (in original order) and nonBlocking contains every id that IS in quarantined (in original order).

tests.description: no quarantined ids: everything is blocking
one quarantined id: split correctly, order preserved

items.explanation: This is exactly L3's routeTests logic, simplified to take the quarantine set directly instead of consulting a module-level registry -- a CI pipeline calls something like this to decide which results can fail the build (blocking) and which only get reported (nonBlocking), preserving each id's original position in its respective list.
items.reference:
🚦 blocking → can fail the build
👁️ nonBlocking → runs, reports, can't fail the build

Why: this is the exact check a CI pipeline runs to decide which results are allowed to gate a merge.

items.prompt: Same routeTests(testIds, quarantined) as before. Confirm it handles an empty testIds list, and that a quarantined id not present in testIds at all has no effect on the result.

tests.description: empty testIds returns empty blocking and nonBlocking
a quarantined id absent from testIds doesn't appear anywhere in the result

items.explanation: The function only ever iterates testIds, so an empty list trivially produces two empty arrays, and a quarantined id that was never actually part of testIds simply never gets visited -- it has no way to leak into either output list.

🚦 blocking → can fail the build
👁️ nonBlocking → runs, reports, can't fail the build

Why: this is the exact check a CI pipeline runs to decide which results are allowed to gate a merge.
